zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, supplied page subset, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); [dataset documentation](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The transcription and physical lineation are based on the supplied BnF scan, not copied from the lexical index.

lines.note: Kiji means returning to a temple, as Teraye cayeru explains. The scan restores the missing ji in the headword; the capital T in Tornarſe and the Japanese term Tera inside the Portuguese gloss are retained.
The example refers respectfully to the priest's return. Padreſamano is one roman Japanese expression here; the OCR incorrectly assigned its initial P to the italic apparatus.

The Japanese honorific verb completes the statement of awaiting the return. The scan supports machimaraſuru, not machinaraſuru, and tornada rather than tornaãa; the Portuguese priest-word continues below.
Dre completes Padre, and a caſa specifies the priest's return home. This is the end of the example, not a new definition.
This separate kiji is an honorific temple-name, paraphrased as tattoqi tera. The Portuguese calls it a holy temple or church; the scan restores both the headword and the badly misrecognized gloss.
The compiler explicitly says the word honours the temple. Tera is a Japanese noun within this Portuguese explanatory sentence; Palaura, not Falaura, is visible.

runs.text: Gallinha do mato, ou perdiz de Iapão.

lines.note: The next kiji is the bird, glossed as woodland fowl or Japanese partridge. The scan reads Gallinha with two l types here, unlike the single-l form on the preceding page.
Kijin is paraphrased through oni and kami and glossed as a devil. The dictionary's religious classification is retained without replacing either Japanese synonym or extending the gloss.
Kijō means returning to a fortress. The scan joins Xiroye, so the OCR's internal space is removed; the caron remains on the headword.
Kimakase is freely doing one's own will. The Portuguese supports the sense of acting according to inclination rather than merely entrusting a task to someone else.
The example characterizes a person who follows his own will. Voluntario is explained by the following liure and need not be read in the modern volunteer sense.
The adjective free completes the preceding characterization. The ampersand is printed and retained on this short continuation row.

Kime, kimuru, kimeta is a verb of sharply reprimanding someone. The scan reads Qime rather than OCR Qune and preserves Portuguese Reprender, without inserting the spelling of the next row's related word.
The example means reprimanding a person. After the paragraph mark, Qi- begins the compound verb Qimetçuquru on the following physical line.
The compound is glossed as having reprimanded or verbally punished someone. Caſtiga- continues below; the printed reprehendido is retained independently of Reprender above.
This completes the translation as punishment by words. It is a verbal-rebuke gloss, not an instruction or a separate physical-punishment entry.
Kimei is a lord's authoritative command, equated with Guioy. The scan reads G rather than OCR C, and separates ſenhor a; q̃ is an abbreviation and is not expanded.

runs.text: ſe não pode deixar de obedecer por ſua auto-

lines.note: The gloss says the command cannot be left unobeyed because of its authority. Auto- belongs to autoridade, not to a separate word.
This completes autoridade and closes the command definition. The short continuation remains a body row.
Kimen is a respected face or presence, paraphrased by tattoqi vomote. The adjective venerauel is divided physically after venera-.

runs.text: uel, ou preſença falando cõ reſpeito. ¶

lines.note: The gloss specifies respectful reference to someone's presence. The example begins Qi-, completing Qimenuo on the next row; this is an indented continuation, not a new entry.
The Japanese refers back to what was said in the addressee's presence. The physical continuation belongs to Qi- above and shares its indentation; Aßi como begins the Portuguese comparison.

The intended sense is having spoken personally to your worship. The scan appears to print o voßa, although a would be expected syntactically; the OCR-supported o is retained as a possible printed anomaly rather than silently emended. The initial verb reads diße.
Kimyō denotes something marvellous. The scan restores the circumflex on the headword and the Portuguese sequence marauilhoſa, not the OCR's maraunlhoſa.
Kimyō fushigi repeats the same marvellous or wondrous sense. Idem is italic reference apparatus, while the entire Japanese expression is roman.
The adjectival form kimyōna is assigned the same meaning. Its -na is part of the printed headword, not supplied editorial morphology.
Kimet is explained through raising and extinguishing or destroying. The Japanese verb reads meſſuru, with two long-s types, correcting OCR meſuaru; the final t of Qimet is retained.
The Portuguese destruction verb completes the paired explanation. Bup. is an upright Buddhist-domain label, including its full stop, not a partly italic word.
This kimi means taste or flavour. The final upright S. marks written usage and distinguishes the entry's apparatus from the following lord-sense.
The second kimi is a lord. The example means attacking or violating one's lord, and the Portuguese begins Matar across the line break.

runs.text: tar ſeu ſenhor, ou aleuantarſe contra elle, &c.

lines.note: The dictionary explains the example as killing one's lord or rising against him. This is a lexical illustration of the preceding Japanese expression.
Kimyō is marked as Buddhist and equated with namu. The following Portuguese explanation describes its function in an invocation; Bup. remains wholly roman.

runs.text: ſe hõra o Fotoque, ou Cami inuocandoo, &c.

lines.note: The invocation honours a Buddha or kami. Fotoque and Cami are Japanese terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation; hõra and inuocandoo retain their printed abbreviation and spelling.
Kimo is glossed through liver, spleen, and related inward parts. After the paragraph mark, ta- begins the soul-word tamaxij in an example of being stunned.
This completes the first expression for becoming stunned. The next Qi- begins another kimo expression; the repeated physical divisions must not be collapsed into one row.
Kimo wo kesu has the same stunned sense. The next expression begins kimo wo hiyasu, divided after fiya-; the Japanese remains roman between italic glosses.
Hiyasu is completed and tçubuſu is offered as an alternative. Idẽ is abbreviated Idem; the following Qimonimei- begins a different expression about impressing something on the heart.
Meizuru completes the Japanese phrase and is explained as penetrating the heart and innermost parts. This is the affective force of the expression, not an anatomical procedure.
Kimo wo iru is glossed as applying diligence and care. Cui- begins cuidado on the following row, and the paragraph mark distinguishes this example from the preceding one.
The care is applied to some matter; a new example then begins kimo ga tçubururu. The actual tçubu- division is kept, as is the tilde on algũa.
The example is completed and an alternative expression follows, both describing astonishment. The scan reads qimoguiyega, without the extra n inserted by OCR.
The alternative gloss is becoming stunned. The scan has ou ficar, with a word space and one f, not OCR oufficar.
Kimoiri denotes a diligent, attentive person in this gloss. The missing letters of diligente and the ampersand before de are restored from the scan.
Great care completes the description of the diligent person. It remains part of Qimoiri rather than the following garment entry.
Kimono is directly glossed as clothing or a garment. This one-line entry is distinct from the following expression containing kimo and the particle no.
Kimo no tabane is explained as the heart or centre of the inward parts. The scan reads Qimono tabane, not Qinono rabane, and ẽtranhas contains an abbreviation tilde whose missing n is not expanded.
Qimot is equated with a vessel or container. The scan restores m in the headword and t in Vtçuuamono; final t and the double u are retained rather than modernized.
The vessel or box is something into which an object is placed. This last body row closes the left column and remains separate from the bottom rule.
Kimu is paraphrased as a returning dream. The Portuguese repeats that explanation; q̃ is left abbreviated and the final S. is an upright written-usage label.
Kin is gold, equated with kogane. The example begins putting gold into mud; the scan joins Qinuo, rather than the OCR's split Q inuo.
The comparison pairs throwing away gold with sinking jewels in deep water. Vo- begins vonaji, the expression of equivalence continued below; xizzumetaruni retains its printed double z.
Vonaji completes the comparison. The source is Taif., book 33, not OCR book 39; the source abbreviation remains roman and the book reference italic.

runs.text: bota o ouro na lama, & as pedras precioſas

lines.note: The translation describes throwing gold into mud and precious stones into a deep pool. This is an illustrative comparison, not a separate entry for jewels.
Pego completes the location of the submerged jewels as a deep pool or deep water. The short Portuguese continuation closes the citation.
This homophonous kin denotes the testicles together with the scrotal sac. The bodily sense is separate from the preceding gold entry.

runs.text: Soalhas, ou ſeſtros de metal. Vt,

lines.note: Another kin is described as metal percussion instruments. The historical terms Soalhas and ſeſtros are retained; the example of sounding them follows.
The alternatives mean making the instrument sound or striking it. Latin l introduces the second verb, and fa- begins fazer on the next row.
The Portuguese completes the explanation as causing the metal instruments to sound. The row belongs to the percussion entry rather than the next stringed-instrument entry.
This kin is equated with koto and described as a musical instrument. The compiler's comparison with a European keyboard instrument continues below without implying identical construction.
Crauo completes the comparison; the example means playing the instrument. The intervening S. is upright, while Vt. and the Portuguese verbs are italic.
The first translation ends, then the second Japanese example concerns tuning or adjusting the instrument. The paragraph mark separates the two examples.
Temperar explains tuning the instrument, not tempering a metal object. The final upright S. marks written usage.
Kina is directly glossed as the colour yellow. The short independent entry is followed by the unrelated regional name Qinai.
Kinai is given with the preferred form Gokinai. The geographical gloss begins within the five regions, with cinco divided after cin-; Meliùs is corrected from OCR Meltùs.

runs.text: co reinos vezinhos ao Miaco, ou estes cinco

lines.note: The five regions are described as neighbouring Miaco, or as those regions themselves. The scan restores reinos, vezinhos ao Miaco, and cinco from the heavily corrupted OCR; Miaco is the Japanese place-name inside the Portuguese sentence.
Reinos completes the second alternative geographical definition. The dictionary's own term is retained rather than replaced with a modern administrative label.
Kinan means grave danger or trouble. The scan-supported internal v in Ayavqi is retained; tra- begins trabalho on the next line.
The example means reaching a state of great danger. Qinanni is one printed word, and the translation's object continues below.
This completes the translation as reaching great danger. The upright S. labels written usage.
Kinbaku is gold leaf. The repeated form begins a gilding example and has an actual terminal hyphen; the OCR's split Q inbacu is removed.

runs.text: uo voqu. l, voſu. l, qinbacude damu.

lines.note: Three alternative expressions describe applying gold leaf. Both l markers mean or and remain separate from the Japanese; the visible damu is retained without substituting a modern verb.
The common Portuguese translation is gilding with gold leaf. This belongs to all the preceding alternatives.
Kinbyō is glossed as gilded folding screens. Beobos is the printed Portuguese form and is not normalized to modern spelling.
Kinbukurin is an edging or border compared to a binding. The gold-coloured or gilded qualification is completed on the following line.
The object or its border is gilded. This completes the preceding definition, rather than introducing a separate general term for gold objects.

runs.text: Peßoa que tem a cabeça calua porter

lines.note: Kinka describes a bald-headed person. The printed porter is retained as one graphic sequence; the cause of the baldness follows below.

runs.text: arrancado todos os cabelos, ou por ſer aſsi na-

lines.note: The hair may have been completely pulled out, or the condition may be natural. The visible mixed aſsi spelling and the physical na- division are retained.
This completes naturalmente, the alternative of natural baldness. The short continuation closes Qinca.
Kinkai denotes a prohibition or injunction. The repeated Japanese imaxime is printed twice and is preserved rather than deleted as a supposed duplication.
Ley supplies law as the alternative gloss, and the example means violating a prohibition. The scan restores the e in ley and joins Qincaiuo.
This completes the example: vocaſu is to break a prohibition or precept. The scan supports the full spelling prohibição, restoring the vowel lost in the draft.

runs.text: Laranjinhas que ſe dão em hũas la-

lines.note: Qincan denotes the small citrus fruit; the Portuguese begins a description of little oranges borne on certain trees. Preserve hũas and the divided la- at the physical right edge.
The continuation completes laranjeiras and says that the orange trees themselves are also small. The printed nasal spelling tãobem is retained rather than modernized to também.

runs.text: Bolſa que ſe traz na cinta. No

lines.note: Qinchacu is a purse carried at the waist. The noun is Bolſa, not the draft's Boſſa; the final No introduces the regional alternative on the next line.

The regional note says that in ximo the purse is called Fôzǒ. The word is part of Portuguese explanatory prose, not a new headword; the scan shows a continuous italic run, with circumflex ô and caron ǒ.
Nixiqino noren identifies rich brocade curtains. The gloss begins Cortinas ricas, split at the physical line end, and the headword's final vowel bears a caron.

runs.text: cas, ou panos de armar de ſeda, ou broca-

lines.note: The curtains are further described as decorative hangings of silk or brocade. Preserve the right-edge broca- division and the printed long ſ in ſeda.
This short line completes brocadilho from broca- above. It remains a separate physical body line, concluding the material description before the next entry.

runs.text: Iuramento que ſe faz batendo na

lines.note: This separate Qinchǒ entry describes an oath made by striking a weapon. The repeated headword is not a duplication error: its explanation differs from the preceding curtain entry.

runs.text: Catana nua com hũa faca, ou outro ferro. Vt,

lines.note: The oath involves striking the bare Catana with a knife or other iron implement. Catana is embedded in the Portuguese sentence, and Vt introduces the Japanese verbal example below.
Qinchǒ ſuru means to take or make this oath. The headword and verb form the roman Japanese example, followed by an italic Portuguese explanation.
Qinchǔ denotes the royal palace. The small mark over u is a caron in the scan, not the grave accent of the draft; Paços is the palace noun, not passos.

runs.text: Boca douro: diz ſe de hum homem

lines.note: The literal expression is a mouth of gold, applied to a man described on the following lines. The scan has a colon after douro, not a final s, and the separate diz ſe is retained.

runs.text: eloquente, & que diz muitas ſentenças, ou

lines.note: The man is eloquent and utters many maxims or sayings. This line continues the same Portuguese definition and ends with ou leading into its final alternative.
The definition ends with good sayings spoken by the mouth. The scan supports ditos and the historical double-l spelling polla, correcting the draft's dutos and plla without modernizing the text.
